mcqs.learning_point: Changing one relevant factor at a time where appropriate
mcqs.question: Which pair of experiments best illustrates the principle of changing only one relevant factor at a time?

options.A: Experiment 1 tests the effect of sunlight on plant growth while keeping water, soil type and temperature constant. Experiment 2 tests the effect of water amount while keeping sunlight, soil type and temperature constant.
options.B: Experiment 1 varies both sunlight and water together. Experiment 2 varies only soil type.
options.C: Both experiments change several factors (light, water, and temperature) at the same time.
options.D: Both experiments keep all conditions the same and do not change any factor.

mcqs.answer: Experiment 1 tests the effect of sunlight on plant growth while keeping water, soil type and temperature constant. Experiment 2 tests the effect of water amount while keeping sunlight, soil type and temperature constant.
mcqs.explanation: Option A follows the scientific method by altering a single variable in each experiment while keeping all other relevant conditions unchanged, allowing any observed differences to be linked directly to the factor being tested. The other options involve changing multiple factors together or not changing any factor, which does not satisfy the principle of changing one relevant factor at a time.

mcqs.question: Why is it essential to keep other relevant conditions controlled in a fair scientific investigation?

options.A: It makes the experiment look more organized for the observer.
options.B: It ensures that any change in the result can be attributed to the factor being tested.
options.C: It allows the researcher to use fewer materials.
options.D: It guarantees that the experiment will always produce the expected outcome.

mcqs.answer: It ensures that any change in the result can be attributed to the factor being tested.
mcqs.explanation: Controlling all variables except the one under investigation isolates the effect of that single variable, so any observed difference in the outcome is due to the variable being tested. Options A, C, and D are unrelated to the scientific purpose of control and may lead to incorrect conclusions.

mcqs.question: What does ‘making repeated observations’ mean in a scientific investigation?

options.A: Observing the phenomenon once and writing a conclusion immediately.
options.B: Observing the same phenomenon several times to check that the results are consistent.
options.C: Changing the experiment each time to see different results.
options.D: Recording observations only when they match the hypothesis.

mcqs.answer: Observing the same phenomenon several times to check that the results are consistent.
mcqs.explanation: Repeated observations help verify that the results are reliable and not due to random chance. Option A lacks repetition, C changes the experiment, and D introduces bias, all of which contradict the principle of repeated observation.

mcqs.question: Why is it important to record the results of an investigation honestly?

options.A: Because it makes the report look longer and more impressive.
options.B: Because honest records allow others to verify the findings and build reliable knowledge.
options.C: Because it helps the investigator remember the experiment for future exams.
options.D: Because it prevents the need to repeat the experiment.

mcqs.answer: Because honest records allow others to verify the findings and build reliable knowledge.
mcqs.explanation: Honest recording ensures transparency and reproducibility, which are core to scientific progress. Options A, C, and D do not address the fundamental reason for honesty in scientific data.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes using results as evidence from stating an opinion?

options.A: Evidence is based on measured data from the investigation, while an opinion is a personal belief not supported by data.
options.B: Both evidence and opinion are equally reliable ways to explain a scientific phenomenon.
options.C: An opinion is a conclusion drawn from data, whereas evidence is a guess before testing.
options.D: Evidence can be changed to fit the hypothesis, while an opinion remains fixed.

mcqs.answer: Evidence is based on measured data from the investigation, while an opinion is a personal belief not supported by data.
mcqs.explanation: Scientific evidence comes directly from systematic observation or measurement, whereas an opinion lacks this empirical support. Options B, C, and D misrepresent the nature of evidence and opinion in science.

mcqs.question: A student tests how quickly two different types of paper absorb water, but only uses one piece of each type and does not repeat the test. Which limitation should the student recognise?

options.A: The experiment did not control the temperature of the room.
options.B: Only two paper types were examined, so the results may not represent all paper varieties.
options.C: The student used too much water, affecting absorption speed.
options.D: The experiment measured the wrong variable.

mcqs.answer: Only two paper types were examined, so the results may not represent all paper varieties.
mcqs.explanation: Testing only two samples limits the ability to generalise findings to other papers; a larger, more varied sample would reduce this limitation. While temperature (option A) could also be a factor, the most direct limitation described is the narrow sample size.

mcqs.question: A class investigates how different amounts of sugar affect the rate of yeast fermentation. What is the primary purpose of this investigation?

options.A: To find the amount of sugar that gives the fastest fermentation rate.
options.B: To prove that yeast can ferment without any sugar.
options.C: To compare the fermentation abilities of different yeast species.
options.D: To measure how temperature changes affect fermentation.

mcqs.answer: To find the amount of sugar that gives the fastest fermentation rate.
mcqs.explanation: The investigation aims to determine the relationship between sugar quantity and fermentation speed, i.e., identifying the optimal sugar level. Options B, C, and D describe different investigations not aligned with the given purpose.

mcqs.learning_point: Changing one relevant factor at a time where appropriate
mcqs.question: Sam wants to study how temperature influences the solubility of salt in water. He prepares three beakers, each containing the same amount of water and the same amount of salt, and stirs each for the same time. He keeps the beakers at 20 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C respectively. Which factor is Sam changing in his investigation?
mcqs.explanation: Sam varies only the temperature while all other relevant conditions (salt amount, water volume, stirring) remain constant, adhering to the principle of changing one factor at a time. Options A, C, and D are kept constant in the experiment.
